remarks: This is an FGD-only record (Mode B); no official ED interview exists for Consent to Establish in Goa to cross-check against.

Participants used the discussion to raise broader ease-of-doing-business concerns (power, water, land infrastructure, environment clearance, NOC processes) beyond Consent to Establish specifically; several findings below concern these parallel/downstream approvals rather than CTE itself, but are retained because participants raised them in the CTE session.

findings.text: Industrial plots allotted for setting up units may lack basic infrastructure such as power, water supply and street lighting at the time of allotment.
Establishing a dedicated transformer connection can involve a high upfront cost to the industry, with the asset later transferring to the electricity department without a corresponding rebate.
Obtaining a new power connection (e.g., 33 KV) to a plot can remain pending for several months without departmental action.
Water availability at newly allotted industrial plots may be limited, requiring dependence on tankers pending pipeline connectivity.
Environment Clearance for an individual unit can take several months, as each company must obtain it separately even where the land was developed by the industrial estate authority.
Sequential, multi-department clearance requirements (e.g., for diesel storage NOC) can extend timelines where department confirmations are not sought in parallel.
Differing interpretation of construction-area thresholds (e.g., built-up area definitions) across departments can create inconsistent Environment Clearance requirements for the same project.

A conflict was noted between a central government notification exempting certain industry categories from mandatory rainwater harvesting and the continuing requirement imposed by state pollution control and environment clearance processes for the same categories.

No overarching single-window policy currently mandates that all approvals required to set up an industry (power, water, environment, fire, etc.) be integrated under one system; each departmental clearance is governed separately, of which Consent to Establish is only one.
Consent to Establish is processed through an online, state single-window system, reducing the need for physical visits in most cases.
Renewal of Consent to Establish is a manual process rather than an automatic renewal, required approximately every three years.
Approvals granted on one department's portal are not automatically recognized by other, related departments, requiring the same file/information to be re-submitted separately at each department.
At a later approval stage (Consent to Operate), sequential review by multiple officials was cited as a source of processing delay.

No specific redundant or duplicate document was identified by participants for the Consent to Establish checklist itself; the required project report and supporting data were generally considered relevant and proportionate.

Once an approval is obtained from one department, the same supporting information sometimes has to be resubmitted afresh to other, related departments due to lack of file-sharing between department portals.
Incomplete or non-compliant documentation was cited as the main reason for delay in the Consent to Establish process itself, requiring correction and resubmission.
At the Consent to Operate stage, sequential review by a large number of officials was identified as contributing to backlog, with increased caution following a fire-related incident.
Move towards a unified single-window clearance system covering all approvals needed to establish an industry, rather than separate departmental portals and fees.
Have the industrial estate authority obtain Environment Clearance for a developed plot in advance, rather than requiring each individual unit to obtain it separately.

Consent to Establish itself was consistently described as simple, transparent and quick when documentation is complete, in contrast to more time- and coordination-intensive downstream approvals (Consent to Operate, Environment Clearance, utility connections).

findings.text: Although the Consent to Operate application is processed online, physical follow-up with the concerned authorities may still be required to obtain updates on the progress of the application.

The online system provides visibility of application status, but limited information on the specific stage through which the application is progressing; status may show only 'in progress' or 'under approval' without stage-wise detail.
Certain related authorizations, particularly waste authorization, continue to be processed through offline mechanisms, without equivalent online tracking, possibly requiring physical visits.

The current Consent to Operate process lacks clearly defined turnaround times for individual stages, creating unpredictability and preventing timely identification/escalation of applications that exceed the prescribed processing period.
The portal provides procedural and checklist information, but clearer visibility of individual processing stages would help clarify application movement.
No major policy-level difficulty with the Consent to Operate process was identified; the overall process was described as online and smooth.
Notifications are not consistently available for movement of the application from one processing stage to another, making it difficult to identify exact status without follow-up.
While Consent to Operate is processed online, related authorizations such as waste authorization follow an offline process, resulting in different tracking and follow-up mechanisms.
No specific requirement for repeated, duplicate, or re-submission of the same documents was identified in relation to the Consent to Operate process.
Limited visibility of application movement and absence of stage-wise notifications may result in the need for follow-up with concerned authorities to ascertain status.
The absence of clearly defined turnaround times for individual stages may make it difficult to determine whether an application has exceeded the expected processing period.
Define and publish stage-wise turnaround times for each stage of the Consent to Operate process on the portal.
Enhance stage-wise application tracking so applicants can identify the stage where an application may be pending beyond the prescribed timeframe.
Strengthen online notifications for important status changes and instances where processing exceeds the defined timeframe, reducing the need for repeated follow-up.
Extend online status-tracking facilities to related authorizations currently processed offline, particularly where absence of tracking requires physical visits.

The Consent to Operate process was generally described as smooth, with online application and status facilities supporting the overall process; expansion/renovation changes were accommodated without significant procedural difficulty.
Some entities engage consultants to manage renewals, testing, compliance requirements and related periodic filings, including activities related to water treatment and pollution compliance.

Participants raised a potential policy overlap between periodic renewal and infrastructure-triggered provisional/final NOC approvals, and suggested the renewal framework be reviewed given parallel annual self-declaration and third-party audit requirements.

findings.text: The online renewal system does not provide an adequate facility to update certain name or organizational changes; such changes require direct coordination with the Fire Department and a separate supporting letter.
The inspection process does not have a consistently predictable timeframe, with some applications reportedly pending for several months, requiring repeated follow-up with the department.
Errors in issued NOCs, particularly regarding names and room-related details, may not be readily corrected through the existing system, requiring repeated office visits.
The annual self-declaration and third-party audit requirements have created uncertainty regarding applicable formats, subsequent procedural steps and timelines after submission.

The existing renewal framework may result in overlapping compliance requirements where fire-safety approvals are already obtained during infrastructure expansion, while a separate periodic renewal requirement continues to apply.

The need for periodic renewal may be examined in cases where compliance is already demonstrated through annual self-declarations, third-party verification and infrastructure-change approvals, to reduce overlapping compliance requirements.
The online renewal system does not provide a dedicated option for name changes, requiring direct coordination with the Fire Department.
The inspection process does not provide a clearly visible stage-wise workflow indicating the expected sequence and status of inspection after submission.

Although third-party audit reports can be submitted online and the auditing agency selected through the portal, subsequent steps after submission are not clearly presented through a defined flow or timeline.
Procedural information and relevant service links may be available across both the department website and the Goa Online portal, requiring users to navigate between sources.
Where an application is rejected after the processing period and subsequently re-applied, the same supporting documents are required to be uploaded again, resulting in duplication of documentation.

Where renewal, infrastructure changes and related fire-safety approvals are undertaken at different stages, separate applications and supporting submissions may be required for the same premises across the regulatory cycle.
The lack of a clearly defined timeframe for completion of inspection may result in applications remaining pending for extended periods and necessitate repeated follow-up.
Applications remaining pending at the end of the processing period may be rejected and require fresh application and re-submission of documents, extending the overall processing cycle.

One reported case involved an approximately six-month period between application and renewal, with continuous follow-up and compliance-related changes, linked to compliance requirements following a fire incident.

Define a one-month timeframe for inspection and NOC issuance, consider deemed release for complete applications beyond the prescribed period, and enable online correction of name and other NOC errors.
Provide a standard stage-wise flowchart and timelines for third-party audits and make the prescribed annual self-declaration format clearly available online.
Provide online contact and appointment facilities to enable clarification and follow-up without repeated physical visits.
The renewal process was reported to be relatively simple where there were no changes in business or NOC details, enabling entities to complete the process directly with limited departmental visits.
The Fire Department's EODB section provides information on applicable fees, procedures, checklists, required documents and indicative approval timelines, supporting clarity.

gaps.text: No official SLA or average renewal-processing timeline is given; inspection timelines are described only as unpredictable, with a proposed (not current) one-month target.
No fee figures or validity/periodicity figures are given for Renewal of Fire NOC.
It is not clear whether a deemed-approval mechanism currently exists; the suggestion to 'consider deemed release' implies none does, but this is not explicitly confirmed.
No document checklist is itemized beyond annual self-declaration, third-party audit report, and (for name/org changes) a separate supporting letter.

A defined one-month inspection/issuance timeframe, deemed release for complete applications beyond the prescribed period, and online correction of NOC errors are suggested but not-yet-implemented reforms.

The renewal process was reported as relatively simple with limited departmental visits where there are no changes in business or NOC details, supported by Goa Online's acknowledgement-based tracking and the Fire Department's EODB informational section.
